slides.title: Just for your interest…

transcription.tex: Why can we not immediately set \(h=0\) in \(\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}\frac{(x+h)^2-x^2}{h}\)?
If we substitute \(h=0\) straight away:\par \(\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}\frac{(x+0)^2-x^2}{0}=\lim_{h\to0}\frac00\).\par Wait: this does not determine the limit.

\(\frac00\) is an indeterminate form.\par Some expressions have limits that grow without bound, such as \(\frac1h\) as \(h\to0^+\). But an indeterminate form alone does not determine a limit.\par Zero divided by a non-zero number is zero; dividing by a number approaching zero can produce unbounded values. These observations do not resolve \(\frac00\).
Can you guess other indeterminate forms: expressions whose limiting values cannot be determined from the form alone?

Thankfully, there are techniques that turn a limit expression into one without an indeterminate form.\par In this example, expand and simplify:\par \(\frac{(x+h)^2-x^2}{h}=2x+h\), for \(h\ne0\).\par Hence \(\lim_{h\to0}(2x+h)=2x\); substituting here is valid. Other techniques are more advanced.\par This is important when sketching harder functions.

transcription.tex: Method 1: Differentiation\par \(f\prime(x)=2x-4=0\).\par \(x=2\).\par \(f(2)=2^2-4(2)+9=5\).\par Therefore the minimum value is 5.
Method 2: Completing the square\par \(f(x)=(x-2)^2+5\).\par Since \((x-2)^2\ge0\), the minimum value of f(x) is 5. This occurs at \(x=2\).
Note: Method 2 applies to quadratic functions. For other functions, use differentiation.

\(y=x^{1/2}-x\).\par \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac12x^{-1/2}-1=0\).\par \(\frac12x^{-1/2}=1\).\par \(x^{-1/2}=2\quad\Rightarrow\quad\frac1{\sqrt{x}}=2\).\par \(\sqrt{x}=\frac12\quad\Rightarrow\quad x=\frac14\).\par When \(x=\frac14\),\par \(y=\sqrt{\frac14}-\frac14=\frac14\).\par The turning point is \(\left(\frac14,\frac14\right)\).
A third type of stationary point is a stationary point of inflection.
A point of inflection is where a curve changes concavity: it curves one way before the point, then the other way after it.
At the point, \(f\prime(x)=0\).\par The tangent is horizontal; the concavity changes.
The terms convex and concave are also used in optics. Terminology varies; the key feature here is the change in concavity.
Here \(f\prime(x)\ne0\).\par Not every point of inflection is stationary.
A stationary point of inflection is sometimes called a saddle point.

transcription.tex: Method 1: Compare the gradient just before and just after the stationary point.
At a minimum or maximum the gradient changes sign. At a stationary point of inflection it is zero at the point without a change of sign.

transcription.tex: 1. [MAT 2014 1C] The cubic\par \(y=kx^3-(k+1)x^2+(2-k)x-k\)\par has a turning point that is a minimum at \(x=1\) precisely for:\par A) \(k>0\)   B) \(0<k<1\)   C) \(k>\frac12\)\par D) \(k<3\)   E) all values of \(k\).

\(\frac{dy}{dx}=3kx^2-2(k+1)x+(2-k)\).\par At \(x=1\),\par \(\frac{dy}{dx}=3k-2k-2+2-k=0\).\par Thus \(x=1\) is stationary for every \(k\). We require a minimum.\par \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6kx-2(k+1)\).\par At \(x=1\), \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=4k-2\).\par For a minimum, \(4k-2>0\), so \(k>\frac12\).\par At \(k=\frac12\), the stationary point is an inflection, so it is excluded. Answer: C.
2. [MAT 2004 1B] Find the smallest value of\par \(f(x)=2x^3-9x^2+12x+3\)\par in the range \(0\le x\le2\).

\(f\prime(x)=6x^2-18x+12=0\).\par Divide by 6: \(x^2-3x+2=0\).\par \((x-1)(x-2)=0\), so \(x=1,2\).\par \(f(1)=8\) and \(f(2)=7\).\par At the start of the interval, \(f(0)=3\).\par Compare all stationary points and endpoints: the minimum value is 3, at \(x=0\).

transcription.tex:
Consider $\mathrm f(x)=ax^3-6ax^2+(12a+12)x-(8a+16)$.
Since $\mathrm f(2)=8$ and $\mathrm f'(2)=12$, the curve $y=\mathrm f(x)$ touches $y=x^3$ at $(2,8)$: notice that both calculations are necessary to prove that the curves touch.
To find the other intersection point, let $\mathrm f(x)=x^3$.
$\Rightarrow(a-1)x^3-6ax^2+(12a+12)x-(8a+16)=0$.
Substituting $x=2$: $8(a-1)-24a+2(12a+12)-(8a+16)=0$.
$\Rightarrow(x-2)[(a-1)x^2-(4a+2)x+(4a+8)]=0$ (notice that factorising by inspection is much easier than using a method such as long division).
Substituting $x=2$ into the quadratic factor: $4(a-1)-2(4a+2)+(4a+8)=0$.
$\Rightarrow(x-2)(x-2)[(a-1)x-(2a+4)]=0$.
So the other intersection point has coordinates $\left(\frac{2a+4}{a-1},\left[\frac{2a+4}{a-1}\right]^3\right)$.
\textbf{(i)} When $a=2$, $\frac{2a+4}{a-1}=8$.
Hence the two graphs touch at $(2,8)$ and intersect at $(8,512)$.
$y=2x^3-12x^2+36x-32$ has no turning points: consider the derivative $6x^2-24x+36=0$.
\textbf{(ii)} When $a=1$, $\frac{2a+4}{a-1}$ is undefined.
Hence the two graphs touch at $(2,8)$ and do not intersect elsewhere.
$y=x^3-6x^2+24x-24$ has no turning points: consider the derivative $3x^2-12x+24=0$.
\textbf{(iii)} When $a=-2$, $\frac{2a+4}{a-1}=0$.
Hence the two graphs touch at $(2,8)$ and intersect at $(0,0)$.
$y=-2x^3+12x^2-12x$ turns when $x=2\pm\sqrt2\approx3.4$ and $0.6$: consider the derivative $-6x^2+24x-12=0$.

transcription.tex: 2. \(f(x)=(x+1)(x-4)^2\).\par a. Sketch the graph of \(y=f(x)\).\par b. On a separate set of axes, sketch the graph of \(y=f\prime(x)\).\par c. Show that \(f\prime(x)=(x-4)(3x-2)\).\par d. Use the derivative to determine the exact coordinates where the gradient function cuts the coordinate axes.

\(f(x)=(x+1)(x-4)^2=x^3-7x^2+8x+16\).\par \(y=0\Rightarrow x=-1\text{ or }4\).\par Stationary points: \(\frac{dy}{dx}=0\).\par \(\frac{dy}{dx}=3x^2-14x+8\).\par \((3x-2)(x-4)=0\Rightarrow x=\frac23\text{ or }4\).\par \(x=\frac23:\ y=(\frac23+1)(\frac23-4)^2=\frac{500}{27}\).\par \(x=4:\ y=(4+1)(4-4)^2=0\).\par Stationary points: \((\frac23,\frac{500}{27})\) and \((4,0)\).\par \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6x-14\).\par \(x=\frac23:\ 6(\frac23)-14=-10<0\), so a maximum.\par \(x=4:\ 6(4)-14=10>0\), so a minimum.

\(\begin{array}{c|c|c}x&f(x)&f\prime(x)\\ x<\frac23&\text{Positive gradient}&\text{Above x-axis}\\ x=\frac23&\text{Maximum}&\text{Cuts x-axis}\\ \frac23<x<4&\text{Negative gradient}&\text{Below x-axis}\\ x=4&\text{Minimum}&\text{Cuts x-axis}\\ x>4&\text{Positive gradient}&\text{Above x-axis}\end{array}\)

transcription.tex: A cuboid has a rectangular cross-section whose length is twice its width, \(x\) cm, as shown in Figure 2. The volume is \(81\text{ cm}^3\).\par The total length of the twelve edges is \(L\) cm.

Let the remaining dimension be \(y\) cm.\par Volume: \(2x^2y=81\), so \(y=\frac{81}{2x^2}\).\par Total edge length:\par \(L=2(2x+x+2x+x)+4y\)\par \(=12x+4y\).\par Substitute for y:\par \(L=12x+4\left(\frac{81}{2x^2}\right)\)\par \(=12x+\frac{162}{x^2}\).
b. Use calculus to find the minimum value of \(L\). (6 marks)
c. Justify, by further differentiation, that your value of L is a minimum. (2 marks)
\(\frac{d^2L}{dx^2}=\frac{972}{x^4}\).\par At \(x=3\),\par \(\frac{d^2L}{dx^2}=\frac{972}{3^4}=12>0\).\par Therefore \(L=54\text{ cm}\) is a minimum.

transcription.tex: 10. A wire frame forms a large rectangle divided into 12 equal rectangles, in six columns and two rows. Each small rectangle has width \(x\) mm and height \(y\) mm. The total length of wire is 1512 mm.
a. Show that the total area is\par \(A=1296x-\frac{108x^2}{7}\text{ mm}^2\). (4 marks)

Three horizontal wires each have length \(6x\). Seven vertical wires each have length \(2y\).\par Total wire length \(=18x+14y\) mm.\par \(18x+14y=1512\).\par \(y=\frac{1512-18x}{14}\).\par Total area: \(A=2y\times6x=12xy\).\par Substitute for y:\par \(A=12x\left(\frac{1512-18x}{14}\right)\)\par \(=1296x-\frac{108x^2}{7}\).
b. Find the maximum area enclosed by the frame. (4 marks)

For a maximum, \(\frac{dA}{dx}=0\).\par \(\frac{dA}{dx}=1296-\frac{216}{7}x\).\par \(1296-\frac{216}{7}x=0\).\par \(x=\frac{7\times1296}{216}=42\).\par When \(x=42\),\par \(A=1296\times42-\frac{108}{7}\times42^2\)\par \(=27\,216\).\par Maximum area \(=27\,216\text{ mm}^2\).\par Check: \(\frac{d^2A}{dx^2}=-\frac{216}{7}<0\), so a maximum.
